THOUGHT: This 62-year-old male presents with two non-healing, erythematous, crusted, firm, painless plaques—one on the penile shaft and one on the left middle finger. The lesions are refractory to prior empiric treatments for syphilis and eczema, and serologic testing confirms absence of active syphilis (and other common STIs including HIV, HBV, HCV). The patient is a heavy, long-term smoker—a major risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). The biopsy finding of nuclear hyperchromasia, multinucleation, and increased mitotic figures within follicle-bearing epithelium is highly characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma in situ (i.e., Bowen disease) or invasive SCC; notably, “follicle-bearing epithelium” implies involvement of epidermis with adnexal structures—consistent with cutaneous SCC rather than basal cell carcinoma or melanoma. While penile SCC is rare overall, it is more prevalent in regions with limited access to circumcision, HPV exposure, chronic inflammation, and smoking—factors potentially relevant given his African origin and smoking history. The synchronous presentation of identical-appearing lesions at two anatomic sites raises concern for either multifocal SCC (e.g., field cancerization in sun-exposed or chronically irritated skin) or, less likely, metastatic disease—but absence of lymphadenopathy and lack of a known primary make metastasis improbable. The finger lesion could represent actinic damage (though not explicitly described as sun-exposed), but more plausibly reflects either independent SCC arising in chronically irritated or HPV-infected skin—or possibly autoinoculation (though uncommon). However, the most parsimonious explanation is multifocal cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma—specifically, Bowen disease (SCC in situ) progressing to invasive SCC, given the crusting, induration, and biopsy features. While penile intraepithelial neoplasia (PeIN) is a precursor, the biopsy description (“follicle-bearing epithelium”, nuclear atypia, mitoses) aligns best with well-documented histopathologic criteria for SCC. Other considerations—such as psoriasis, lichen planus, or mycosis fungoides—are unlikely given lack of scale (psoriasis), absence of pruritus or characteristic Wickham striae (lichen planus), and no epidermotropism or cerebriform lymphocytes on biopsy (MF). The negative STD panel rules out secondary syphilis (which can mimic SCC but would show plasma cells on histology and positive serology) and chancroid (which is painful and ulcerative). Thus, the constellation of age, smoking, non-healing crusted plaques at high-risk sites (penis + digit), and biopsy showing malignant keratinocyte proliferation strongly supports cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.

DIAGNOSIS: Squamous cell carcinoma
